name: Prejudice
description: Prejudice is a pre-judged evaluation of a social group or its members, where category membership drives liking, dislike, suspicion, or threat perception before individual evidence does. In practice it is broader than one single bias effect: it bundles attitudes, feelings, and judgment tendencies toward groups.
design_relevance_note: Highly relevant to inclusive design, trust and safety, recommendation systems, hiring/internal tools, persona work, and model evaluation. Category-based liking, distrust, or threat judgments can leak into segmentation, policy, copy, and automation.
prevalence_note: Foundational in social psychology and common in inclusive-design, fairness, trust-and-safety, and responsible-AI work, but not usually taught as a day-to-day interaction-design heuristic in the same way as anchoring or Hick's Law.

findings.description: Reviewing contemporary prejudice research, Amodio and Cikara treat prejudice as a real intergroup evaluative construct that shapes categorization, stereotype formation and updating, perception, emotion, decision making, and self-regulation. The reviewed literature keeps prejudice conceptually distinct from stereotyping and discrimination while showing that the three regularly interact in practice.

applications.title: A Jena University preschool program reduced children's early stereotyping through increased intergroup contact
applications.description: Researchers at Jena University, led by Dr. Andreas Beelmann, developed a program for pre-school-aged children that increases their contact with children from different social, ethnic, or gender groups -- aiming to prevent a natural in-group-favoring bias from developing into stereotyping and prejudice against other groups later in life.
applications.ethical_note: A genuinely prosocial application of behavioral research, not a designed influence on a user for commercial gain -- relevant to any platform or product design context (education technology, children's media, community/social features) that has an opportunity to structure early intergroup contact rather than reinforce in-group-only social defaults.

applications.title: Kalla & Broockman's pre-registered replication that door-to-door conversations reduce prejudice -- after the original study was retracted for fraud
applications.description: A 2014 Science paper (LaCour & Green) claiming that brief door-to-door conversations durably reduced prejudice toward gay people was retracted after LaCour was found to have fabricated the underlying data. Rather than abandoning the hypothesis, researchers Joshua Kalla and David Broockman ran a new, pre-registered study (hypotheses and analysis code registered in advance at egap.org, full data/code publicly released, an independent professor verifying the data was genuinely collected) and found that high-quality canvassing conversations about transgender rights durably reduced prejudice.
applications.ethical_note: This is as much a meta-science case study as a prejudice-reduction one, and worth keeping both readings visible: a real, high-profile psychology finding was fabricated and retracted, but the underlying real-world question it asked was legitimate enough that other researchers re-tested it properly (pre-registration, open data, independent data-collection verification) and found genuine support -- a concrete illustration of science self-correcting rather than a reason to distrust every canvassing-reduces-prejudice claim.

applications.title: The 2018 Yale 'napping while Black' incident as an illustration of prejudice-driven suspicion
applications.description: In May 2018 at Yale University, a White student called campus police to investigate a Black graduate student who was napping in a common area of her own dormitory. UCLA social psychologist Tiffany Brannon discusses this alongside two similar 2018 incidents (a Black student eating lunch at Smith College prompting a police call, and Black students being pulled off a graduation stage at the University of Florida for a celebratory dance) as evidence of how implicit and explicit prejudice can drive perceptions of who 'belongs' in ordinary, everyday spaces.
applications.ethical_note: This entry documents a real, independently corroborated instance of the underlying psychological phenomenon (prejudice) rather than a product, interface, or business decision -- matching the precedent already set by this corpus's research-integrity entries (the Ariely/Wertenbroch and Walach retraction cases) for grounding a bias in a concrete, dated, real-world event rather than requiring a digital product. There is no persuasion or design dimension to grade here; it exists to keep 'Prejudice' from staying a purely abstract entry in this corpus.
